chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Bakr ibn Salih, from the one who mentioned it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

A man congratulated another man who had been blessed with a son, saying: 'Congratulations to you — may he become a horseman!' So al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said to him: 'What knowledge do you have that he will be a horseman or a foot-soldier?'

The man said: 'May I be sacrificed for you! Then what should I say?' He said: 'Say: You have given thanks to the Bestower, and may blessings be upon you in the endowment (the child), and may he reach full maturity, and may you be graced with his righteousness.'

key_terms.أشده: Full strength/maturity — Quranic term (46:15, 12:22) for when a person reaches physical and moral completeness
key_terms.الموهوب: The endowment — the child given by God, using the same root as الواهب to emphasize the gift relationship
key_terms.الواهب: The Bestower — a divine attribute emphasizing that children are gifts from God, not human achievements
key_terms.بره: Righteousness/filial piety — the quality of being dutiful and good to one's parents and others

ai.seo_question: What is the proper Islamic congratulation for the birth of a son?
ai.summary: Imam al-Hasan (peace be upon him) corrected a man who offered congratulations on the birth of a son by wishing that the child would become a horseman — a presumptuous assumption about the child's future. The Imam taught that the proper Islamic formula for congratulating a new parent focuses on three elements: gratitude to God who bestowed the child, blessings in raising the child, and a prayer for the child's righteous adulthood. This exchange reflects early Islamic etiquette norms where words of congratulation were carefully calibrated to acknowledge divine agency rather than human aspiration.
